title: The Race to Make Pictures Move
summary: In 1888 a Frenchman in England filmed his family walking in a garden for about two seconds, then mysteriously vanished. Soon Thomas Edison's helpers built a peephole movie machine, and in Paris the Lumière brothers showed films on a big screen to a paying crowd. Lots of inventors in different countries raced to make pictures move, and together they invented the movies.

sections.heading: Two Seconds in a Leeds Garden
paragraphs: It is a cool Sunday in October 1888, in the garden of a large house called Oakwood Grange in Roundhay, a leafy part of Leeds in the north of England. Four people are walking on the lawn in a slightly odd way, turning in circles, coats flapping, as if someone has asked them to keep moving. Facing them, mounted on a sturdy wooden stand, is a strange box with a crank. Behind it stands a tall Frenchman named Louis Le Prince. When he turns the handle, a strip of film inside jerks past the lens again and again. He is not taking one photograph. He is taking a whole series of them, one after another.

The result, now called Roundhay Garden Scene, was filmed on 14 October 1888. It lasts only about two seconds. Yet it is generally considered the oldest surviving motion picture. The people in it were Le Prince's son Adolphe, his father-in-law Joseph Whitley, his mother-in-law Sarah Whitley, and a family friend, Annie Hartley. Sadly, Sarah Whitley died just ten days later, so these few seconds of her walking in the garden are an unexpected memorial.

Louis Le Prince was born in Metz, in eastern France, in 1841. He studied painting and chemistry and learned about photography as a young man. In 1866 he moved to Leeds to work for a brass-founding company run by his friend John Whitley, whose sister Elizabeth he married. The couple later ran a school of applied art, and they became known for a method of fixing colour photographs onto metal and pottery. Le Prince also spent several years in the United States, where he became fascinated by the idea of capturing motion.

His first design, patented in 1888, was a machine with 16 lenses, each taking a picture in turn. It was clumsy, because each lens saw the scene from a slightly different position, making the picture wobble. So he built a camera with a single lens that moved a strip of sensitized film in jerks, stopping it briefly for each exposure. For Roundhay Garden Scene he used Eastman paper-based film, the kind you met in Part 9. Adolphe later said the camera ran at 12 frames per second, though modern experts who have studied the surviving frames think it may have been closer to 7.

That same autumn Le Prince filmed traffic crossing Leeds Bridge, with horse-drawn carriages and people on foot moving across the frame, and he filmed Adolphe playing an accordion. The original paper negatives did not survive. In the 1930s, the Science Museum in London made copies on glass of 20 frames of Roundhay Garden Scene, and those copies are how we can still watch it today. Le Prince's surviving films and equipment are now looked after by the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford, not far from Leeds.

sections.heading: The Man Who Vanished
paragraphs: By 1890 Le Prince was ready to show his invention to the world. His wife and children had moved to New York, and he planned to join them to exhibit his work in the United States. First he visited his brother in Dijon, in eastern France. On 16 September 1890 he boarded a train from Dijon heading toward Paris, where friends were expecting him. He never arrived. Neither he nor his luggage was ever found, and no one has ever been able to prove what happened to him. French authorities eventually declared him dead in 1897.

Because Le Prince disappeared just before he might have become famous, people have been arguing about his fate ever since. Some have suggested that rivals who wanted his invention out of the way were involved, and his family suspected Thomas Edison's side because of the patent battles that later followed. Others have wondered whether he chose to disappear because of money troubles, or whether he took his own life. In 2003 researchers found a photograph in the Paris police archives of a drowned man from 1890 who looked somewhat like Le Prince, but others have argued that the man was too short to be him. None of these theories has been proved. The honest answer is that the mystery is unsolved.

His son Adolphe later testified in an American court case about who had first invented motion picture cameras, hoping to win recognition for his father, but the court did not accept Le Prince's work as evidence in the way the family hoped. Adolphe himself died young a few years later. For decades Le Prince was mostly forgotten outside Leeds, and the credit for inventing cinema went to bigger names. Only in the twentieth century did historians rediscover how early and how clever his work had been. Leeds now proudly honours him as a local hero, and a plaque on Leeds Bridge remembers the films he made there.

sections.heading: Edison's Idea and Dickson's Hands
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, in the busy laboratory of the world's most famous inventor, a similar dream was taking shape. In October 1888 Thomas Edison filed a caveat (a kind of early notice to the patent office announcing an idea he was working on) describing a machine that would “do for the Eye what the phonograph does for the Ear.” Edison had invented the phonograph in 1877, so it seemed natural to him that pictures, like sounds, might be recorded and played back. In March 1889 he gave the machine a name: the Kinetoscope, from Greek words meaning “motion” and “to watch.”

Edison was busy with many projects, from electric lighting to iron-ore mining, so he handed the job to one of his most talented assistants, William Kennedy Laurie Dickson. Dickson was born in 1860 in Brittany, France, to a Scottish father and an American mother. As a young man he wrote to Edison asking for a job, was turned down, came to America anyway and was finally hired at Edison's Menlo Park laboratory in 1883. He was a skilled photographer, an engineer and an artist, exactly the mix of talents the project needed. Historians agree that Dickson and his assistants did most of the hands-on experimental work on Edison's motion pictures between 1889 and 1892, while Edison took most of the public credit.

The first experiments copied the phonograph a little too closely. Dickson and his team tried placing rows of tiny photographs in a spiral around a cylinder, which turned while a viewer looked at the pictures through a microscope-like eyepiece. Around 1889 the team made some test films this way, including a short clip known as Monkeyshines, in which a lab worker in a white costume moved around clumsily. The pictures were tiny, blurry and hard to light. A cylinder simply could not hold enough images big enough to be clear.

The breakthrough was switching to a long strip of Eastman's new transparent celluloid film. Edison had travelled to Paris for the great Exposition of 1889, where he met Étienne-Jules Marey, whose chronophotography you met in Part 8 and who was already capturing motion on strips. Back in New Jersey, the team turned to the strip approach. On 20 May 1891, about 150 members of the National Federation of Women's Clubs visiting Edison's laboratory peered into a prototype Kinetoscope and saw a short film of Dickson himself bowing, smiling and taking off his hat. That film, Dickson Greeting, is one of the earliest motion pictures made in America.

sections.heading: The Kinetograph, the Kinetoscope and 35mm Film
paragraphs: Edison's system had two machines. The camera was the Kinetograph, a heavy box driven by an electric motor, so heavy that it mostly stayed in one place. Inside, a toothed wheel called a sprocket gripped the film, pulled one section into position behind the lens, held it still while a shutter let in light, then pulled the next section into place. It did this about 40 times a second, much faster than the 16 or so frames per second that later became common for silent films.

The film strip itself was the team's most lasting contribution. Dickson settled on a strip 1⅜ inches wide, almost exactly 35 millimetres, cut from Eastman film. Along each edge of each frame ran four small rectangular holes, the sprocket holes, so the gears could move the film with precision. Each frame was about one inch wide and three-quarters of an inch tall. This exact format, 35mm film with four perforations per frame on each side, became the world standard for motion pictures and remained the main professional film format for more than a century. If you ever see a reel of old Hollywood film, it is almost certainly a direct descendant of Dickson's strip.

Why such an odd width? Nobody is completely sure. A popular story says Dickson's team simply slit 70-millimetre Eastman rolls down the middle, but film historians say that tale does not hold up. Whatever the reason, nobody was thinking about creating a world standard; they were solving the problem in front of them. But because Edison's films spread around the world, and because other inventors wanted their machines to show Edison films too, many chose the same width and hole pattern. A practical shortcut in a New Jersey workshop became the shape of cinema for generations.

The viewer was the Kinetoscope, a wooden cabinet about as tall as a person's chest. Inside, a loop of film roughly 50 feet long wound endlessly around a series of spools. An electric lamp shone up through the film, and a spinning wheel with a narrow slit let the viewer glimpse each frame for a split second as it passed. You bent over and looked down through an eyepiece on top, like peeking into a box of secrets. A film lasted around 20 seconds, then looped back to the start. Only one person at a time could watch.

The completed system was shown publicly at the Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences on 9 May 1893. The star film was Blacksmith Scene, in which three men, really Edison employees playing blacksmiths, hammer on an anvil and pass around a bottle. Edison did not pay to protect the Kinetoscope with patents in most other countries, a decision historians still argue about. That allowed others, such as the British instrument maker Robert W. Paul, to build copies and then their own film cameras.

sections.heading: The Black Maria and the First Kinetoscope Parlor
paragraphs: Films need light, lots of it. Early film was not very sensitive, and electric lights of the time were too weak to light a scene well. So in December 1892 workers at Edison's laboratory complex in West Orange, New Jersey, began building the world's first film studio, finished in 1893. It was a long, narrow wooden shed covered in black tar paper, with a section of roof that could be swung open to let in sunshine. The entire building sat on a circular track, a turntable, so it could be rotated during the day to follow the sun across the sky. Inside, walls painted black made the performers stand out brightly against a dark background.

Dickson and his colleagues nicknamed the building the Black Maria, after the slang name for police wagons of the time, because both were black, cramped and stuffy. Performers of every kind came to West Orange to be filmed: dancers, acrobats, boxers, comedians, trained animals and strongmen. One of the most famous early films made there is Fred Ott's Sneeze, from early 1894, in which an Edison employee takes a pinch of snuff and sneezes for the camera. The studio closed in 1901, when Edison moved film production to a new glass-roofed studio in New York City, and the old building was torn down in 1903. A replica was built on the site in 1954, and the National Park Service reopened it to visitors in April 2024.

Being filmed in the Black Maria was a strange experience. Performers had to squeeze their act into a small patch of floor in front of the camera, which could not move, and finish it in well under a minute, because that was all the film a single take could hold. In 1894 the famous strongman Eugen Sandow flexed his muscles there, and the sharpshooter Annie Oakley fired her rifle at glass balls. Dancers twirled long skirts, two cats were filmed in a tiny boxing ring, and real boxers fought rounds shortened to fit the film. These little films were not stories. They were moving snapshots of acts that people might otherwise pay to see in a theatre.

With a studio full of films, it was time to make money. On 14 April 1894 the Holland Brothers opened the first commercial Kinetoscope parlor at 1155 Broadway in New York City. It had ten Kinetoscope machines arranged in two rows of five, each showing a different film. For 25 cents a customer could watch every machine in one row, or for 50 cents, both rows. That was not cheap, but crowds lined up anyway. Within months, Kinetoscope parlors opened in Chicago, San Francisco, London and other cities, and Edison's company sold hundreds of machines.

The excitement did not last. Once people had seen the novelty of a 20-second film through a peephole, many did not come back, and the second year's profits fell by more than 95 percent. Edison tried to revive interest in 1895 with the Kinetophone, a Kinetoscope with a phonograph inside that played music through ear tubes, but the sound was not truly synchronized with the pictures and only about 45 were made. Edison believed the money was in selling machines to parlors, one viewer at a time. Other inventors were already betting on a different idea: throwing the moving picture onto a big screen so a whole room of people could watch together.

sections.heading: Projectors Appear in Many Countries
paragraphs: Projecting moving pictures sounds simple, but it was harder than it looks. A projector needed a bright light, a strong mechanism to move the film in jerks without tearing it, and a way to avoid melting or setting fire to the film with the heat of the lamp. During 1894 and 1895, inventors in the United States, Britain, France and Germany were all racing to solve these problems, often without knowing about each other.

In the United States, Charles Francis Jenkins showed a filmed motion picture to an audience in his hometown of Richmond, Indiana, in June 1894. In New York, the Latham family, with Dickson secretly advising them while he still worked for Edison, built a projector called the Eidoloscope and on 20 May 1895 showed a film of a boxing match to a paying audience, one of the earliest commercial film projections anywhere. The Lathams also developed a clever trick, a slack loop of film above and below the gate, still known as the Latham loop, that kept long films from snapping as they were jerked along.

In Berlin, two brothers named Max and Emil Skladanowsky built a projector called the Bioscop. Their solution to flicker was unusual: the Bioscop had two lenses and two strips of film, and it showed frames from each strip alternately, so one picture was always appearing while the other strip moved. The film was 44.5 millimetres wide and had no sprocket holes like Edison's. On 1 November 1895 they presented the Bioscop at the Wintergarten, a grand music hall in Berlin, as part of a three-hour variety show. Their program lasted about 15 minutes and included eight very short films, played over and over, such as acrobats, a folk dance and a boxing kangaroo.

In Britain, Robert W. Paul and the photographer Birt Acres made a camera in 1895 and filmed scenes such as waves crashing on the shore. Paul then designed his own projector, which he showed in London early in 1896. Each of these inventors could claim to be among the first to project films. That is exactly why historians say that no single person invented the movies: the technology grew in many places at once, with each team borrowing ideas, making mistakes and sometimes racing to patent offices.

sections.heading: The Lumière Brothers and the Grand Café
paragraphs: The inventors who usually get the most attention for this moment were two brothers from Lyon, in France: Auguste Lumière, born in 1862, and Louis Lumière, born in 1864. Their father, Antoine, was a painter and photographer who started a business making photographic plates. Louis, while still a teenager, improved the recipe for dry plates, and the Lumière factory in the Monplaisir district of Lyon grew into one of the biggest makers of photographic plates in Europe. The family had money, chemistry skills and machine workshops, a perfect combination for building a film machine.

Antoine had seen Edison's Kinetoscope in Paris in 1894 and urged his sons to do better. The brothers, with Louis leading the technical work, designed a machine they called the Cinématographe, borrowing a name first used by another French inventor, Léon Bouly, in 1892. They patented it on 13 February 1895. It was ingenious: a single hand-cranked wooden box that worked as a camera, then, with a few changes, as a printer to copy the film, and then, with a lamp behind it, as a projector. A small claw-like mechanism driven by a cam pulled the film down one frame at a time, using one round sprocket hole on each side of each frame. It weighed only about 7 kilograms, small enough to carry anywhere, which meant operators could film real life in streets, stations and gardens rather than in a studio.

The Cinématographe ran at about 15 to 16 frames per second, much slower than Edison's camera, which saved film. A typical roll was about 17 metres long, enough for roughly 50 seconds. The brothers' most famous early film, Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory, shows dozens of employees, many of them women in long skirts and hats, pouring out of the factory gates in Lyon, followed by a man on a bicycle and a dog. Three versions were filmed in 1895. One was shown privately on 22 March 1895 in Paris to about 200 members of a society for encouraging French industry, who were astonished.

Then came the famous evening. On 28 December 1895 the Lumières held a paid public screening in the Salon Indien, a basement room of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris. Only a small audience, a few dozen people, came to that first show; tickets reportedly cost one franc. The program had ten short films, each less than a minute long, and the whole show was over in well under half an hour. It included workers leaving the factory, blacksmiths at work, a baby being fed breakfast, people swimming in the sea and a little comedy in which a boy steps on a gardener's hose, the gardener gets sprayed in the face and then chases the boy. That comedy, later known as L'Arroseur arrosé, is often called the first fiction film comedy.

Word spread quickly, and soon queues stretched down the boulevard. In 1896 Lumière operators carried Cinématographes around the world, filming and screening in London, New York, Buenos Aires, Egypt and many other places, and bringing home pictures of distant cities. Many people in many countries saw their very first moving pictures thanks to a Lumière operator. Curiously, the brothers themselves are said to have called cinema “an invention without any future,” and they had mostly stopped making films by 1905 to concentrate on other projects, including the Autochrome colour plates you will meet in Part 13.

You may have heard that when the Lumières showed their film of a steam train pulling into the station at La Ciotat, the audience screamed and ran away from the screen. That story is a legend. The train film was not even on the program of 28 December 1895, and historians have found no reports written at the time describing a panic. Some viewers certainly found the approaching train startling and thrilling, but there is little evidence that anyone fled.

sections.heading: Edison Catches Up: The Vitascope
paragraphs: Back in the United States, Edison's company had fallen behind on projection, so it bought its way back in. In 1895 two young inventors, Thomas Armat and Charles Francis Jenkins, modified Jenkins's projector, the Phantoscope, and demonstrated it at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta. The partners soon quarrelled, each claiming to be the true inventor. Armat sold the rights to his version to the businessmen Norman Raff and Frank Gammon, who sold Edison's Kinetoscopes. They made a deal with Edison: his company would manufacture the projector, and it would be marketed under Edison's famous name as the Vitascope.

On 23 April 1896 the Vitascope had its first theatrical showing at Koster and Bial's Music Hall in New York City, as part of a vaudeville show. Huge images of dancers, a comic boxing scene and waves breaking on a beach, filmed in England by Robert Paul's partner Birt Acres, flickered onto a screen while a band played. Newspapers raved, and the waves especially impressed the audience. Within a few months, Vitascopes were touring many American cities. But only about 20 films were available, and competition from the Lumière Cinématographe and other projectors was fierce. By late 1896 Edison's company had introduced its own projector, the Projectoscope, and stopped selling the Vitascope.

So who invented the movies? Le Prince filmed the first surviving moving pictures in Leeds. Dickson and the Edison team created the 35mm film strip and the first film studio. The Lathams and Jenkins showed early projections in America, the Skladanowskys in Germany, Paul and Acres in Britain, and the Lumières turned the Cinématographe into a worldwide sensation. Many inventors in several countries contributed, and none of them could have done it without Eastman's celluloid film. There is still one question left, and it is a strange one. Every one of these films is just a row of still photographs. So why does your brain see a man bowing, a train rolling and waves crashing, instead of a stack of frozen pictures?

deepDive:
Ask 'who invented cinema?' and the answer depends on what you count as cinema. If it means recording a sequence of photographs on a strip with a single camera, Louis Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene of 14 October 1888 is the oldest surviving example. If it means a practical system of camera, film format and viewer, the Edison laboratory's Kinetograph and Kinetoscope, built largely by W. K. L. Dickson between 1889 and 1893, have the strongest claim. If it means projected films for a paying audience, the Lathams' Eidoloscope (20 May 1895, New York) and the Skladanowskys' Bioscop (1 November 1895, Berlin) both came before the Lumières' famous show of 28 December 1895. French tradition and many textbooks still celebrate the Lumière date, because the Cinématographe was portable, reliable and quickly spread worldwide, and because its programme looks like a real film show.

Technical numbers reveal very different design choices. Edison's camera ran at about 40 frames per second, using lots of film per second of action, while the Lumières recommended about 15 to 16 frames per second; at 16 frames per second a 17-metre roll gave roughly 800 frames, about 50 seconds. Edison's 35mm film had four rectangular perforations on each side of every frame, while the Lumière film had a single round hole per side. Edison's format won, partly because his films circulated so widely, and 35mm with four perforations per frame remained the main professional film standard for more than a century.

Credit was shaped by business and law. Edison put his name on Dickson's work and on the Armat–Jenkins projector he sold as the Vitascope. Armat and Jenkins quarrelled for years over who invented their machine. Edison's company later fought a long series of patent lawsuits to control American filmmaking, and Le Prince's family tried, unsuccessfully, to use those courts to win recognition for him. His disappearance in 1890 remains unexplained, and claims that he was murdered are speculation, not established fact. Modern historians, such as those who have studied Dickson's papers, have worked to restore credit to the people who did the hands-on engineering.
funFact: The oldest surviving motion picture, Roundhay Garden Scene from 1888, lasts only about two seconds, and the original film is lost; it survives because the Science Museum in London copied 20 of its frames onto glass in the 1930s.
